title: Health Checkups in Edmonton: A Practical Guide to Preventive Care
seoTitle: Health Checkups in Edmonton: A Preventive Care Guide
description: Plan your next health checkup in Edmonton. Learn what to discuss about blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, screening, vaccines, and preventive care.

blocks.text: A health checkup is an opportunity to step back from individual symptoms and consider your health more broadly. You might want to understand your blood pressure, review a prescription, discuss a family history of illness, or find out which screening tests apply to you. The most useful visit starts with your circumstances, not a standard list of tests for everyone.

For adults looking for health checkups in Edmonton, preparation can be straightforward. Bring your questions, explain what has changed, and ask your healthcare provider to help identify the priorities. You do not need to arrive with your own diagnosis or a request for every available investigation.

This guide explains subjects worth discussing at a preventive-care appointment and how to turn that conversation into a practical plan. Recommendations should be tailored by a qualified healthcare professional to your age, history, symptoms, and individual risks.
What is the purpose of a preventive health visit?

Preventive care focuses on the steps that are appropriate for your health before a problem becomes the main reason for seeking help. Edmonton Doctors lists routine health review, screening discussions, blood pressure and risk checks, medication review, and ongoing health planning within its [checkup services](/services/checkups-physicals/). [^18]
A useful way to prepare is to ask yourself three questions: What has changed? What am I concerned about? What would I like to understand better?

Your answer might be a family member's recent diagnosis, uncertainty about a screening invitation, or difficulty following an existing treatment plan. These are meaningful starting points, even when you do not feel acutely unwell.
Let the clinic know the purpose of the appointment when booking. A general preventive discussion, a new symptom, and an employment medical may require different arrangements.
Does every adult need an annual physical?

Not necessarily. Choosing Wisely Canada advises that healthy adults do not automatically need a complete physical every year. The timing of visits and investigations should reflect individual needs, including symptoms, ongoing conditions, medication monitoring, and recommended preventive services. [^9]
That does not mean preventive care is unimportant. It means the appointment should have a useful purpose rather than being organised around an automatic testing routine.

Ask your doctor what follow-up schedule makes sense for you and what changes should bring you back sooner. Someone receiving treatment for an ongoing condition may need a different schedule from someone without symptoms or significant risk factors.

Rather than asking only, “Am I due for my annual physical?” consider asking, “Which preventive services and reviews am I due for now?” That question keeps the discussion focused on your actual care needs.
Start with your history and recent changes

Prepare a short summary of significant medical conditions, operations, medications, allergies, and relevant family history. These are among the types of information included in Alberta's physician record standards when applicable. [^7]

Also write down changes you have noticed since your last visit. Include when they started, whether they are continuing, and how they affect everyday activities. Be clear when a symptom is new rather than something you have already discussed and monitored.

For family history, bring what you know about the condition, which relative was affected, and their approximate age at diagnosis. Do not delay an appointment because you cannot reconstruct every detail.
If you have several concerns, state them at the beginning and ask how to prioritise them. This makes your expectations visible and gives you a chance to agree on what needs attention first.
Blood pressure: ask what your readings mean

Blood pressure measures the force of blood against artery walls. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of problems such as heart attack and stroke. It often has no obvious symptoms, which is why feeling well does not replace appropriate measurement. [^19][^20]

If you have a reading you do not understand, bring it to the appointment. Include when and where it was taken and whether you have other readings for comparison. Your clinician may recommend repeat measurements or home monitoring to clarify the pattern. [^20]

Ask what range applies to your circumstances, whether further checks are needed, and how results should be recorded. If home monitoring is recommended, request instructions about the device, cuff fit, and measurement technique.
Avoid changing prescribed treatment because of one number you have interpreted yourself. Ask the clinician what the result means and what action, if any, is appropriate.
Cholesterol: look at the wider cardiovascular picture

A cholesterol blood test can measure several blood fats, including total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. These results help clinicians evaluate cardiovascular risk and, when relevant, response to treatment. [^21]

The wider discussion matters as much as an isolated laboratory number. MyHealth Alberta identifies factors such as blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, age, and family history as relevant to cardiovascular risk assessment. [^22]

Ask whether testing is appropriate for you and how the result would affect your care. You can also ask which changes are likely to matter most in your particular situation, rather than trying to copy someone else's treatment plan.
If you have had recent blood work elsewhere, mention it before repeating tests. Bring the date and location, and ask whether the existing results can inform the current review.
Blood sugar: discuss your individual diabetes risk

Blood sugar assessment may be appropriate depending on your symptoms and risk factors. Type 2 diabetes evaluation can involve blood glucose testing or an A1c test, alongside a medical history and clinical assessment. Family history, previous gestational diabetes, and other health factors can influence the discussion. [^23]

An A1c test reflects average blood sugar over roughly the previous two to three months. Whether it is suitable, how a result should be interpreted, and whether confirmation is needed are questions for your healthcare provider. [^24]
Tell your clinician about previous abnormal results or monitoring already underway. Ask when reassessment is appropriate rather than assuming everyone needs the same testing frequency.

If you already have diabetes, clarify whether the appointment is for general prevention or condition-specific follow-up. Your healthcare team can identify the monitoring and reviews relevant to your established care plan.
Cancer screening: check what applies to you

Screening is intended for people without symptoms who meet the relevant eligibility criteria. Alberta's [Screening for Life resources](https://screeningforlife.ca/) describe breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer screening, with additional information about lung screening. Eligibility and the appropriate test depend on the screening programme and individual circumstances. [^25]

At your checkup, ask which screening you are due for, which previous results matter, and whether your family history changes the usual approach. Bring any screening reminders you have received and mention tests completed outside your current clinic.

It is also important to distinguish screening from investigating symptoms. Tell your clinician about a new concern rather than treating a routine screening appointment as the answer to every possible problem.
For cervical screening, ask which test and interval apply under current Alberta guidance. Avoid relying on an old schedule or assuming another person's recommendations are the same as yours.
Review vaccinations and previous records

Preventive care can include checking your immunization history and discussing recommended vaccines. MyHealth Alberta provides information about adult immunization, routine schedules, pregnancy, travel, and seasonal vaccines. Recommendations and access depend on the vaccine and the person's circumstances. [^26]

Bring the records you have, especially if some vaccinations were received elsewhere. Ask which doses can be confirmed, whether anything needs updating, and where an appropriate appointment should be arranged.

Mention planned travel or a change in your health circumstances before assuming your usual schedule covers every situation. Check availability and eligibility directly rather than assuming every vaccine is stocked at the family medicine clinic.
If you cannot locate old records, ask how to proceed. A missing document is a reason to seek guidance, not to guess whether a vaccine is needed.
Include mental health, sleep, and everyday functioning

A checkup can also be a time to raise concerns about mood, anxiety, stress, sleep, or difficulty coping with daily responsibilities. Edmonton Doctors lists [support for stress, mood, and anxiety concerns](/services/mental-health-support/), along with care planning and referral guidance. [^27]

You do not need a diagnostic label to start the conversation. Try describing the change: “I am struggling to sleep,” “I have stopped enjoying things,” or “Work is becoming difficult to manage.” Add how long this has been happening and what support you have already tried.
Ask what kind of assessment or follow-up would be appropriate. If talking about the subject feels difficult, write a brief note before the visit and use it to begin.
A routine appointment is not the right place to wait for help during an immediate crisis. Seek urgent assistance when there is immediate danger.
Make medication review a practical conversation

Bring a list of prescriptions, non-prescription medicines, vitamins, and supplements. Include what you actually use and any questions about taking it. Medication review is one of the services described on the Edmonton Doctors checkup page. [^18]
Useful questions include: What is each medicine intended to do? Is monitoring needed? What should I do if I miss a dose? How should I request a renewal? Are there problems I should report promptly?
Be honest about difficulties with cost, timing, swallowing tablets, or remembering doses. The appointment is more useful when the clinician understands what is happening in practice.

Do not change or stop a prescribed medicine simply because you have concerns after reading online. Bring those concerns to the prescriber or pharmacist and ask for advice about your specific situation.
Choose health goals that fit your life

Primary Care Alberta's prevention resources include physical activity, healthy eating, immunization, screening, and support to reduce tobacco and alcohol-related harms. These are areas you can discuss according to your needs and priorities. [^28]

For the appointment, choose one or two goals you would genuinely like help with. Perhaps you want a realistic activity plan, ideas for meals during rotating shifts, or support with reducing tobacco use.

Describe the barriers as well as the goal. “I want to be more active, but my knee hurts” is a different conversation from “I do not know where to start.” Similarly, a food budget or unpredictable schedule is useful context, not a personal failure.
Ask for a first step that is clear enough to try and a way to review how it went. A workable plan is more valuable than leaving with a long list you cannot realistically follow.
Blood tests should answer a useful question

More tests are not automatically better. Choosing Wisely Canada's family medicine guidance recommends against annual screening blood tests unless they are indicated by the person's risk profile. It also cautions against investigations that are unlikely to benefit the patient. [^29]
When a test is suggested, ask what it is checking and how the result could affect your care. When a test is not recommended, ask why it would not be useful in your circumstances.

Follow any preparation instructions provided by the ordering clinician or laboratory. Ask whether fasting is needed and how to manage regular medications rather than changing your routine without guidance.
Leave with a clear follow-up plan

Before the appointment ends, confirm what has been decided. Which tests, if any, need arranging? Is another visit required? How will you receive results? What should you do if a concern changes before the next review?

Keep a short record of the agreed actions and any timeframe discussed. If you are unsure who is responsible for arranging something, ask directly rather than assuming the clinic or another service will contact you.
You can also ask how to revisit a concern that could not be fully addressed that day. Preventive care does not require every question to be settled in one appointment.
The useful outcome is a plan you understand, with a clear next step and a way to follow up.
Discuss preventive care with an Edmonton family doctor

Edmonton Doctors provides information about family medicine, health checkups, and [chronic disease management](/services/chronic-disease-management/), including blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar follow-up. Review the relevant service page and contact your preferred clinic to ask about appointment options. New patients can use the [registration pathway](/register/) to request follow-up about availability. [^30]

For North and Northeast Edmonton options, the website lists Beverly Medical Center & Walk-In on 118 Avenue and Balwin Medical Centre on 127 Avenue. Beverly can be reached at [(780) 522-1236](tel:+17805221236) and Balwin at [(587) 415-1251](tel:+15874151251). Confirm which location and appointment type are appropriate before attending, particularly when requesting a specific physician or service. [^4]

Start with the questions most relevant to your life now. A thoughtful checkup is not about collecting the most tests. It is about understanding your health, choosing appropriate preventive care, and knowing what to do next.
